pos: n. (proper name; a prince of Simeon in Hezekiah's day)
etymology: Hebrew Ya'aqobah, heel-catcher or supplanter, a form of Jacob, from 'aqab, to take by the heel.
biblical_def: Jaakobah is one of the princes of Simeon who led the tribe's expansion in the days of Hezekiah. “And Elioenai, and Jaakobah, and Jeshohaiah, and Asaiah, and Adiel, and Jesimiel, and Benaiah” (1 Chronicles 4:36). “These mentioned by their names were princes in their families: and the house of their fathers increased greatly” (1 Chronicles 4:38). Needing land for their flocks, “they went to the entrance of Gedor, even unto the east side of the valley, to seek pasture for their flocks” (1 Chronicles 4:39). “And these written by name came in the days of Hezekiah king of Judah, and smote their tents” (1 Chronicles 4:41), and dwelt there. Jaakobah's name is a form of Jacob, the father of all the tribes. Simeon had been the tribe Jacob rebuked for its cruelty at Shechem, and it dwindled in the wilderness; yet in Hezekiah's day its princes, a Jacob among them, found room to grow. God's discipline of a tribe was not His abandonment of it.

pos: n. (proper name; a prince of Simeon in Hezekiah's day)
etymology: Hebrew Yeshochayah, the LORD humbles, from shachah, to bow down, and Yah.
biblical_def: Jeshohaiah is one of the Simeonite princes whose families increased greatly. “And Elioenai, and Jaakobah, and Jeshohaiah, and Asaiah, and Adiel, and Jesimiel, and Benaiah” (1 Chronicles 4:36). “These mentioned by their names were princes in their families: and the house of their fathers increased greatly” (1 Chronicles 4:38). In Hezekiah's days they took the pastures near Gedor, and a further band “even of the sons of Simeon, five hundred men, went to mount Seir” (1 Chronicles 4:42). “And they smote the rest of the Amalekites that were escaped, and dwelt there unto this day” (1 Chronicles 4:43). Saul had been commanded to destroy Amalek and had failed; in Hezekiah's day the sons of Simeon finished the work against the remnant. Jeshohaiah's name means the LORD humbles. The LORD humbled the proud Amalekite, the first nation to attack Israel after the exodus, by the hand of Israel's smallest tribe.

pos: n. (proper name; a prince of Simeon in Hezekiah's day)
etymology: Hebrew Yesimi'el, God sets or God establishes, from sum, to set, to place.
biblical_def: Jesimiel is a prince of Simeon named in the list of those whose house increased greatly. “And Elioenai, and Jaakobah, and Jeshohaiah, and Asaiah, and Adiel, and Jesimiel, and Benaiah” (1 Chronicles 4:36). The Chronicler explains why these names were kept: “These mentioned by their names were princes in their families” (1 Chronicles 4:38). They moved to the valley near Gedor in Hezekiah's days and drove out the former occupants, “and dwelt in their rooms: because there was pasture there for their flocks” (1 Chronicles 4:41). Jesimiel's name means God sets, or God establishes. The Simeonites found a place because God set them there. Jacob had prophesied that Simeon would be scattered in Israel, and the tribe's portion was always within Judah's; yet in the days of a godly king, God gave its princes room and settled them. He sets the solitary in families and appoints the bounds of His people.

pos: n. (proper name; a prince of Simeon; also a son of Rehoboam)
etymology: Hebrew Ziza', abundance or shining; the sense is uncertain.
biblical_def: Ziza is the name of two men in Chronicles. The first is a prince of Simeon whose lineage is traced back six generations: “And Ziza the son of Shiphi, the son of Allon, the son of Jedaiah, the son of Shimri, the son of Shemaiah” (1 Chronicles 4:37). He was among the princes whose house “increased greatly” (1 Chronicles 4:38) and who took new pasture in Hezekiah's days. The second Ziza is a son of king Rehoboam by Maachah, Absalom's daughter: “which bare him Abijah, and Attai, and Ziza, and Shelomith” (2 Chronicles 11:20). Rehoboam “loved Maachah the daughter of Absalom above all his wives and his concubines” (2 Chronicles 11:21), and made her son Abijah chief. He gave his other sons fenced cities and “desired many wives” (2 Chronicles 11:23). Ziza son of Rehoboam was a prince passed over for his brother. One Ziza led a growing tribe; the other was a king's son in a household divided by many wives.

pos: n. (proper name; a Benjamite, son of Elpaal)
etymology: Hebrew Yishmeray, the LORD keeps, from shamar, to keep, to guard.
biblical_def: Ishmerai is a Benjamite of the house of Elpaal. “Ishmerai also, and Jezliah, and Jobab, the sons of Elpaal” (1 Chronicles 8:18). The house of Elpaal was a builder's house: “The sons of Elpaal; Eber, and Misham, and Shamed, who built Ono, and Lod, with the towns thereof” (1 Chronicles 8:12). Its men also fought: Beriah and Shema were heads of the inhabitants of Aijalon, “who drove away the inhabitants of Gath” (1 Chronicles 8:13). The long Benjamite list ends with the note, “These were heads of the fathers, by their generations, chief men. These dwelt in Jerusalem” (1 Chronicles 8:28). Ishmerai's name means the LORD keeps. Benjamin was nearly destroyed in the war of Judges 20, reduced to six hundred men; the God who keeps His people preserved the tribe until its chief men dwelt in Jerusalem itself, beside the house of God.

pos: n. (proper name; a Benjamite, son of Elpaal)
etymology: Hebrew Yizli'ah, preserved or drawn out; the sense is uncertain.
biblical_def: Jezliah is a Benjamite, son of Elpaal, named with his brothers Ishmerai and Jobab. “Ishmerai also, and Jezliah, and Jobab, the sons of Elpaal” (1 Chronicles 8:18). Elpaal's sons included builders of towns and warriors: Beriah and Shema “were heads of the fathers of the inhabitants of Aijalon, who drove away the inhabitants of Gath” (1 Chronicles 8:13). Aijalon was the valley where the sun stood still for Joshua, and the men of Benjamin there held the border against the Philistines. The genealogy of Benjamin closes with the summary that all Israel “were reckoned by genealogies; and, behold, they were written in the book of the kings of Israel and Judah, who were carried away to Babylon for their transgression” (1 Chronicles 9:1). Jezliah's name stands in a list compiled before the exile and preserved through it. The registers of Israel survived the captivity because God would bring His people back.

pos: n. (proper name; a Benjamite, son of Shashak)
etymology: Hebrew Yishpan, he will hide or bald; the sense is uncertain.
biblical_def: Ishpan is a Benjamite of the house of Shashak. “And Ishpan, and Heber, and Eliel” (1 Chronicles 8:22) begin the list that ends, “These were the sons of Shashak” (1 Chronicles 8:25). Shashak himself was a son of Beriah, of the family that “drove away the inhabitants of Gath” (1 Chronicles 8:13), and was named with “Ahio, Shashak, and Jeremoth” (1 Chronicles 8:14). Shashak's sons were eleven, and the whole company stands under the Chronicler's verdict, “These were heads of the fathers, by their generations, chief men. These dwelt in Jerusalem” (1 Chronicles 8:28). Ishpan's name may mean he will hide. The men of Benjamin who settled in Jerusalem dwelt in the city God chose for His name. The smallest tribe, the tribe of the first king, shared the holy city with Judah, and from it came Mordecai, who saved the Jews in Persia, and Saul of Tarsus, the apostle to the Gentiles.

pos: n. (proper name; a Benjamite, son of Shashak)
etymology: Hebrew Yiphdeyah, the LORD redeems, from padah, to ransom, to redeem, and Yah.
biblical_def: Iphedeiah is a Benjamite, the last-named son of Shashak. “And Iphedeiah, and Penuel, the sons of Shashak” (1 Chronicles 8:25). The list of Shashak's sons runs through eleven names (1 Chronicles 8:22–25), and the house was counted among the “heads of the fathers, by their generations, chief men” who “dwelt in Jerusalem” (1 Chronicles 8:28). Iphedeiah's name is a confession: the LORD redeems. The verb padah is used of God redeeming Israel from the house of bondage and of the ransom of the firstborn. It sums up the whole history of Benjamin: a tribe nearly cut off for its sin at Gibeah, spared, restored, carried into exile with Judah, and brought back. The returned exiles read this list knowing that God had redeemed them from Babylon as He once redeemed their fathers from Egypt. “So all Israel were reckoned by genealogies” (1 Chronicles 9:1), and their names were written as the names of a ransomed people.

pos: n. (proper name; a Benjamite, son of Jeroham)
etymology: Hebrew Ya'areshyah, the LORD nourishes or whom the LORD gives; the sense is uncertain.
biblical_def: Jaresiah is a Benjamite, son of Jeroham. “And Jaresiah, and Eliah, and Zichri, the sons of Jeroham” (1 Chronicles 8:27). Jeroham's sons are the last family listed before the Chronicler's summary: “These were heads of the fathers, by their generations, chief men. These dwelt in Jerusalem” (1 Chronicles 8:28). After the exile, the Benjamites of Jerusalem were counted again, and a son of Jeroham appears among them: “And Ibneiah the son of Jeroham” (1 Chronicles 9:8). The house of Jeroham thus spans the exile, named before it and after it. Jaresiah's name may mean the LORD nourishes. God fed His people in the wilderness, sustained them in captivity and brought them back to dwell in the city of His name. The return was itself a nourishment of faith: the same houses that had dwelt in Jerusalem before the exile dwelt there again.

pos: n. (proper name; a Benjamite ancestor of Meshullam)
etymology: Hebrew Yibniyah, the LORD builds, from banah, to build, and Yah.
biblical_def: Ibnijah is a Benjamite ancestor in the line of Meshullam, among those who dwelt in Jerusalem after the exile. “And Ibneiah the son of Jeroham, and Elah the son of Uzzi, the son of Michri, and Meshullam the son of Shephathiah, the son of Reuel, the son of Ibnijah” (1 Chronicles 9:8). The chapter opens: “So all Israel were reckoned by genealogies; and, behold, they were written in the book of the kings of Israel and Judah, who were carried away to Babylon for their transgression” (1 Chronicles 9:1). Then: “And in Jerusalem dwelt of the children of Judah, and of the children of Benjamin” (1 Chronicles 9:3). The verse names Ibnijah four generations back from Meshullam, and closes, “All these men were chief of the fathers in the house of their fathers” (1 Chronicles 9:9). Ibnijah's name means the LORD builds, and the list records exactly that: God building again the houses of His people in the city He had judged. He is distinct from Ibneiah named in the same verse.
